arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Waxman stated the EPA has consistently interpreted the Clean Air Act for thirty years. He argued the law requires setting standards solely by reference to pollutant presence in the air. He emphasized the agency's long-standing interpretation of the statute.

The government contends the Clean Air Act mandates setting standards based only on health effects. the sides that brought the case argue the statute allows considering economic costs. The Court must decide which interpretation aligns with the law.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on how the EPA sets National Ambient Air Quality Standards. the sides that brought the case claim the agency must weigh economic costs. The government argues the statute mandates standards based solely on pollutant presence.

paragraphs: Does the Clean Air Act authorize the EPA to consider economic costs when setting air quality standards?

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether the EPA can weigh economic costs when setting air quality standards. The outcome shapes how the agency balances public health and economic impact. It defines the scope of federal regulatory power over air pollution.
